Indigent

IN-di-juhnt · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Indigent is poor, poverty-stricken, or needy.

After the factory closed, entire blocks of the mill town slid into indigent poverty within a single year.

Worked Example

The lawyer took the case for free, as she often did for indigent clients who could never otherwise afford legal representation.

Someone with essentially no money to cover life's most basic needs, like legal help, is exactly what indigent describes.

How Strong Is It? — struggling → indigent → penniless

struggling vs. indigent

struggling vs. indigent: having a hard time financially, without necessarily lacking basic needs

penniless vs. indigent

penniless vs. indigent: having literally no money at all

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — indu-

prefix — indu-: in (Latin)

root — -igere (egere)

root — -igere (egere): to need, to lack (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Indigent comes from Latin indigere, 'to need' or 'lack,' built from indu- ('in') plus egere ('to need'). Someone indigent is, at the root, a person genuinely lacking what they need.

Use the root in a new word: indigence

Use the root in a new word: indigence: The charity's annual report described a sharp rise in indigence across the region since the factory closed.

Root Check

Word Choice

Indigent describes a person's poverty directly. It connects naturally to pittance (earlier in this unit): being paid a pittance for long enough is one common path into becoming indigent.
